intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy-2 (CHN2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MPZ gene (159440) on chromosome 1q23.3.

paragraphs.text: Congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy is a rare condition. Onset of hypotonia, paresis, and areflexia is prenatal, neonatal, or in early infancy. On histopathology, myelin sheaths are absent or thin. Most of the few reported patients have died within the first years of life (Smit et al., 2008). Smit et al. (2008) noted that mutations had been described in the MPZ, EGR2, PMP22, and MTMR2 genes.

checks.evidence_quote: Congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy is a rare condition

checks.evidence_quote: characterized by prenatal, neonatal or early infantile onset of hypotonia, paresis and areflexia.

checks.claim: On histopathology in congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy, myelin sheaths are absent or thin.
checks.evidence_quote: Histopathologically there are no or thin myelin sheaths.

checks.claim: Most of the few reported patients with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy have died within the first years of life.
checks.evidence_quote: Most of the few patients described in literature die within the first years of life.

checks.evidence_quote: Mutations have been described in the following genes, MPZ, EGR2, PMP22, and MTMR2.

paragraphs.text: Ono et al. (1982) described a Japanese boy with congenital hypomyelination who was 3 years 11 months old. He had delayed motor development and generalized muscle hypotonia and weakness. Tendon reflexes were absent because of peripheral neuropathy. His mental development was normal. Nerve conduction velocities could not be measured. On right sural nerve biopsy, most myelinated fibers had no myelin at all. Electron microscopy showed onion bulbs around the fibers. These were formed by concentric double-layered sheets of basement membrane with fragments of Schwann cell cytoplasm. The authors noted that these features were similar to those of previously reported cases.

paragraphs.text: Tachi et al. (1998) described a male patient with a Dejerine-Sottas disease phenotype. On sural nerve biopsy, fibers were hypomyelinated without active demyelination, and there were onion-bulb formations made of 2 parallel layers of basement membrane. This pathology was consistent with congenital hypomyelination neuropathy (CHN), but his clinical features were more severe than those of previously reported CHN patients.

paragraphs.text: Phillips et al. (1999) reported long-term prospective follow-up of 2 unrelated girls with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy. The first girl presented with neonatal hypotonia and extremely slow nerve conduction velocities. Sural nerve biopsy showed profound hypomyelination without inflammation or myelin breakdown. At age 9 years her motor function was still improving, but follow-up nerve conduction velocities were unchanged.

paragraphs.text: Mandich et al. (1999) described the clinical, morphologic, and immunohistochemical features of a patient with congenital hypomyelination (CH). They characterized CH as a hereditary demyelinating peripheral neuropathy with onset in early infancy, distal muscle weakness, hypotonia, areflexia, and severely slowed nerve conduction velocities. The authors noted that the patient's clinical features were quite distinct from those of CMT1B or Dejerine-Sottas syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Tachi et al. (1998) studied a male patient with a Dejerine-Sottas disease phenotype whose nerve pathology was consistent with CHN. In this patient they identified a GGCA insertion at nucleotide 560 of the MPZ gene. The insertion was a small direct tandem duplication in exon 4, which encodes the transmembrane domain. It shifted the reading frame and created a stop codon. The mutation was not found in either parent. The authors suggested that mutation of the transmembrane domain probably has the largest effect on P0 function.

paragraphs.text: Warner et al. (1996) suggested that CMT1B, Dejerine-Sottas syndrome, and congenital hypomyelination may not be distinct pathophysiologic entities. Instead, they proposed that these disorders form a spectrum of related 'myelinopathies' caused by an underlying defect in myelination. They hypothesized that the differences in clinical severity among MPZ mutations depend on the type of mutation and its effect on protein function, that is, loss of function versus a dominant-negative effect.

paragraphs.text: In their patient with complete absence of peripheral myelin, Charnas et al. (1988) found that Schwann cells proliferated, migrated, ensheathed axons, and produced basal lamina, and then stopped proliferating normally. However, the Schwann cells failed to lengthen spirally and to grow longitudinally. The distance between Schwann cell nuclei was very short, causing marked Schwann cell hypercellularity, and the Schwann cells took on many morphologic features of unmyelinated nerves. Immunocytochemistry detected none of the peripheral myelin proteins P0, P1, or MAG. The authors concluded that the defect appeared to be an arrest of Schwann cell differentiation at the stages of mesaxon elongation and longitudinal growth.

paragraphs.text: Wrabetz et al. (2000) studied transgenic mice that overexpressed P0. On Western blot analysis, P0 overexpression dysregulated other myelin proteins even in the absence of dysmyelination. In P28 Tg80.3 nerves with ultrastructurally normal myelin, P0 was overexpressed by about 60%, MBP was reduced by about 50%, PMP22 was reduced by 35%, and tubulin was unchanged. The authors concluded that Schwann cells sense P0 overexpression and respond by dysregulating other myelin proteins before the threshold for dysmyelination is exceeded.

paragraphs.text: Wrabetz et al. (2000) noted that several features of the P0-overexpressing mice resembled human congenital hypomyelination neuropathy. These included profoundly reduced nerve conduction velocities (1-2 m/s), little active myelin destruction or onion-bulb formation, and redundant basement membrane. Low-level P0 overexpression produced transient hypomyelination, which resembled a subset of reversible CHN. The authors suggested that P0 overexpression represents a new mechanism of hereditary neuropathy. They also suggested that MPZ overexpression might contribute to the pathogenesis of the EGR2 mutation that likely disinhibits Krox 20.

Leg muscles showed angulated and atrophic fibers suggestive of denervation, without fiber type grouping.

paragraphs.text: In P28 sciatic nerve from high-copy Tg80.2 mice, Wrabetz et al. (2000) found marked hypomyelination with an increased number of Schwann cell nuclei. Every transverse section contained bundles of unsorted naked axons of mixed caliber. Schwann cells were surrounded by pockets of redundant basal lamina containing collagen. There were no onion bulbs and little evidence of active demyelination or axonal degeneration. The authors concluded that the dysmyelination resulted from developmental delay rather than myelin destruction. Tg80.2 sciatic nerves contained virtually no myelin at P5 and P14. In the P10 quadriceps nerve, fewer than 1% of axons in a 1:1 relationship with Schwann cells were myelinated, compared with virtually 100% in wildtype mice. The motor branch of the femoral nerve was more dysmyelinated than the sensory branch.

paragraphs.text: Wrabetz et al. (2000) showed that the severity of dysmyelination paralleled Mpz dosage. Mice with 0 to 10 copies (Tg80.3; 0.3-fold overexpression) behaved normally and had normally myelinated nerves at P28. Mice with 10 to 20 copies (Tg80.4; 0.8-fold) had mild tremor, a nerve conduction velocity of 11 m/s, and about 50% of large axons unmyelinated. Mice with more than 20 copies (Tg80.2; 7.3-fold) had evident tremor, weak grip strength, a conduction velocity of 2 m/s, and severe hypomyelination with delayed axonal sorting. Breeding the mildly affected Tg80.3 line to homozygosity raised overexpression from 30% to 80% and produced tremor and dysmyelination. Crossing Tg80.4 into a homozygous Mpz-null background returned myelination to essentially normal. From these experiments, the authors placed the threshold for dysmyelination between 30 and 80% Mpz overexpression (130 to 180% of total Mpz expression). They concluded that the phenotype depended only on Mpz dosage, not on an ectopic effect or a structural alteration of the transgenic P0.

paragraphs.text: Tachi et al. (1998) studied a male patient with a Dejerine-Sottas disease phenotype whose sural nerve pathology was consistent with congenital hypomyelination neuropathy. In this patient they identified a GGCA insertion at nucleotide 560 of the MPZ gene. The insertion was a small direct tandem duplication in exon 4, which encodes the transmembrane domain. It shifted the reading frame and created a stop codon. The mutation was not found in either parent.
